en.title: Master of Public Administration (MPA): the whole course
en.short: What an MPA covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What public administration is
sections.text:
Public administration is the study of how governments and public agencies are organised and how they carry out public decisions. It covers the executive branch, public services, and the rules and resources that make implementation possible. It draws on political science, economics, law, management and ethics. An MPA prepares graduates for management and policy work in government, international organisations, nonprofits and firms that deal with the public sector. It is applied: theory matters because it helps you judge what will work in a real institution. It is not only about paperwork; it is about how public authority is used and controlled.

The degree is often confused with the Master of Public Policy. Both overlap, but an MPA usually gives more weight to management, organisation and implementation, while an MPP gives more weight to policy analysis and evaluation. Check the curriculum, because titles vary.

sections.heading: How the programme is usually organised
sections.text: An MPA is a master’s degree. Awards and lengths differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a master’s programme is commonly one to two years full-time, and part-time study takes longer; universities set credit units and dissertation rules under national guidelines. In the United Kingdom, many MPA courses are one year full-time. In the United States, many are two years full-time. These are common patterns, not universal rules. Check your own handbook for the award title, credit units, internship or placement requirements, and the dissertation or capstone. Ask whether your programme is taught, research-based, or mixed. Some programmes require an internship or a work-based project. Teaching may be in the evening or at weekends for working students. Accreditation and quality assurance also differ; in Nigeria the National Universities Commission oversees university programmes, but the details are in the university handbook.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text: Teaching usually starts with foundations: the history and theories of public administration, and organisational theory and design in the public sector. You then study the public policy process and policy analysis and decision tools. Economics comes next, including public sector economics, public budgeting and the budget cycle, public financial management and control, public sector accounting and reporting, and public procurement and contract management. Management subjects follow: human resource management, administrative law, ethics and accountability, governance, intergovernmental relations and local government, service delivery and citizen engagement, public-private partnerships, e-government, performance management, strategic management, leadership and change, and public sector reform. Later topics include programme evaluation, quantitative methods, research methods, comparative public administration, development administration, and nonprofit and civil society management. The capstone project brings these together. A typical sequence moves from foundations to tools, then to sector management, then to synthesis. Not every programme covers every topic in the same depth, and some offer electives.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Study by applying ideas to real cases. For each theory, ask what problem it solves and what evidence supports it. Read official documents: budgets, audit reports, procurement notices and service charters. Practise writing short policy memos and briefing notes, because MPA work is often written advice under time pressure. Learn the quantitative tools by doing calculations, not only reading them. Keep a file of country examples, and name the country when you use a rule. Start your capstone early, and use your research methods course to shape the question. Use past questions if they are available, and compare your answer with the marking guide or feedback. Work in a small group to test each other on definitions and cases.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: A common mistake is to treat public management as identical to private management. Public managers answer to law, politics and public scrutiny, not only to owners. Another is to learn definitions without application. Students also use one country’s law or budget rule as if it were universal. Others ignore quantitative methods because they fear numbers, then struggle with evaluation and budgeting. Poor referencing and late capstone work cause avoidable loss of marks. Another error is to write an essay that lists reforms without explaining why they succeeded or failed. Finally, do not describe a reform without saying what problem it addressed and what evidence shows it worked.

keyPoints: An MPA is a master’s degree in the management of public organisations and public programmes.
Programme length, award title and requirements differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
The core areas are foundations, policy, economics and finance, management, law and ethics, governance, and research.
Public management differs from private management because law, politics and public scrutiny shape decisions.
Study by applying theory to real cases and official documents, and practise writing short advice.
Start the capstone early and use research methods to define a clear question.

en.title: Foundations of Public Administration
en.short: Defines public administration, its scope, politics and management links, bureaucracy and public values.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Public administration is the study and practice of how government and public bodies organise work, make decisions, use public money and deliver services under law. Its scope covers central and local government, agencies, public enterprises and some nonprofit bodies that carry out public tasks. Public management is the narrower managerial side: planning, organising, staffing and controlling public services. Politics concerns who governs and which values and choices prevail. The traditional politics-administration dichotomy, linked to Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow, said administrators should simply execute political decisions. Most modern scholars reject a sharp separation: administrators advise, exercise discretion and shape policy in implementation.

sections.heading: Bureaucracy and organisation
sections.text: Classical views treat bureaucracy as a rational, rule-based form. Max Weber described legal-rational authority, hierarchy, written rules and impersonal office-holding. Henri Fayol stressed management functions and principles; Frederick Taylor stressed efficiency through scientific management. Modern perspectives add informal organisation, incentives, culture and networks. They note that rules can protect fairness but can also become rigid. Public administration also draws on organisation theory, but that is treated separately in this course.

sections.heading: Public interest and roles
sections.text: The public interest is the common good that public decisions should serve, but its content is contested: it may mean majority welfare, fair procedure, or protection of vulnerable groups. Core public values include legality, accountability, impartiality, equity, efficiency, transparency and responsiveness. Public administrators act as policy advisers, service managers, implementers and stewards of public resources. A made-up case: Adaeze, a district health officer in Nigeria, must follow procurement rules, answer to elected officials and get medicines to clinics. She balances political direction with legal limits and patient need.

keyPoints: Public administration is the study and practice of government organisation, decisions, resources and services under law.
Public management is the narrower managerial side of public administration.
Politics and administration overlap; the sharp dichotomy is no longer widely accepted.
Weber’s legal-rational bureaucracy rests on hierarchy, written rules and impersonal authority.
Public interest and public values are contested but central to administrative judgement.
Public administrators advise, implement, manage services and steward public resources.

en.title: Organisational Theory and Design in the Public Sector
en.short: Classical, human relations, systems and contingency views, and how public agencies are structured.

sections.heading: Four approaches
sections.text: Organisational theory explains how work is divided, coordinated and controlled. Classical theory, linked to Max Weber and Frederick Taylor, values clear hierarchy, written rules and specialised tasks. Weber called rule-based administration bureaucracy. Human relations theory, linked to Elton Mayo, stresses that informal groups, motivation and supervision shape behaviour. Systems theory sees an agency as open to its environment: inputs become outputs through processes, with feedback. Contingency theory holds that no single design fits all; structure should fit task, technology, size and environment.

sections.heading: Structure and control
sections.text: Structure is the pattern of units, authority and reporting lines. Coordination is how units align their work, through plans, meetings or shared information systems. Control is how managers check performance and correct drift. Span of control is the number of staff reporting to one manager. A narrow span gives close supervision but adds layers; a wide span cuts layers but demands clear rules and capable staff. Public agencies often combine functional units, such as finance and human resources, with programme or area offices. Design choices include centralisation versus decentralisation, specialisation versus generalist teams, and line versus staff authority. Line authority gives direct commands; staff authority gives advice.

sections.heading: Case and design choices
sections.text: Consider a made-up state health agency. Its director must decide whether to organise by function or by district. A functional design pools expertise but slows cross-unit coordination. A district design brings services closer to citizens but may duplicate support staff. Contingency thinking suggests matching design to the agency’s main uncertainty. If local needs vary, give districts more discretion and keep finance central for control. If the task is routine, a classical hierarchy may work. Systems thinking reminds managers that changes in one part, such as new reporting rules, affect the whole agency.

keyPoints: Classical theory relies on hierarchy, rules and specialisation.
Human relations theory shows that informal groups and motivation affect performance.
Systems theory treats an agency as open to its environment and feedback.
Contingency theory says structure must fit task, technology, size and environment.
Span of control is the number of staff reporting to one manager; narrow spans add layers.
Public managers choose between centralisation and decentralisation, and between functional and area-based designs.

en.title: The Public Policy Process: Stages, Actors and Models
en.short: Agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation, with actors and models.

sections.heading: The policy cycle
sections.text: Public policy is a government’s chosen course of action on a public problem. The policy cycle is a teaching model with stages: agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation. Agenda setting is how an issue reaches government attention. Formulation designs options. Adoption is the authoritative decision, by cabinet, legislature or another body. Implementation is delivery by agencies. Evaluation judges outcomes against aims. The stages overlap and loop; a failed evaluation can reopen the agenda.

sections.heading: Actors and institutions
sections.text: Actors include elected politicians, civil servants, courts, interest groups, experts, media and citizens. Institutions shape who gets access and where proposals can be blocked. A federal constitution, for example, creates multiple veto points. Implementation is not automatic: street-level bureaucrats, such as teachers and nurses, adapt rules in daily work. Top-down studies focus on control; bottom-up studies focus on frontline discretion. Policy outcomes also depend on budgets, law and administrative capacity.

sections.heading: Explaining policy change
sections.text: Models simplify complex causation. Rational comprehensive model assumes clear goals and full information, which is rare. Incrementalism, linked to Charles Lindblom, sees policy as small adjustments to existing practice. Kingdon’s multiple streams model says change happens when problem, policy and politics streams join in a window. The advocacy coalition framework sees competing coalitions held together by beliefs. Punctuated equilibrium explains long stability broken by sudden change.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: A made-up health ministry wants to cut maternal deaths. Media reports open the agenda. Officials, midwives and NGOs formulate options. Cabinet adopts a plan. District clinics implement it, and nurses adapt it to local conditions. A survey and clinic records evaluate results. If outcomes disappoint, the issue returns to the agenda.

keyPoints: The policy cycle has five common stages: agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation.
The cycle is a heuristic, not a strict sequence; stages overlap and feedback occurs.
Official and unofficial actors, and institutions, shape which issues reach decision and what is adopted.
Rational comprehensive and incremental models offer contrasting views of decision-making.
Multiple streams, advocacy coalition and punctuated equilibrium explain agenda windows and change.
Implementation depends on street-level discretion, budgets and administrative capacity, and evaluation can restart the cycle.

en.title: Policy Analysis and Decision Tools
en.short: Policy problems, objectives, options, cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness analysis, risk and stakeholders.

sections.heading: Problem and objectives
sections.text: Policy analysis is a way to help a public decision-maker choose. Start by defining the policy problem: the gap between the present situation and a desired one, supported by evidence, and bounded so it is not too broad. Then specify objectives. Good objectives are specific, measurable, time-bound and state whose welfare matters. For example, a city may aim to cut average bus journey time by 15% within two years without raising fares. Clear objectives make later appraisal possible.

sections.heading: Options and appraisal
sections.text: Identify options: status quo, regulation, subsidy, public provision or partnership. Appraise each against criteria: effectiveness, efficiency, equity and feasibility. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) values costs and benefits in money and compares their present values: the worth today of future amounts, after discounting. Net present value (NPV) = present value of benefits − present value of costs. Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) = present value of benefits ÷ present value of costs. A positive NPV and a BCR above 1 support a project, subject to distributional and risk concerns.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A transport authority appraises a bus lane. Present value of benefits is 18 million and present value of costs is 12 million. NPV = 18 − 12 = 6 million. BCR = 18 ÷ 12 = 1.5. The lane passes both tests. If benefits cannot be monetised, use cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA): cost per unit of outcome = cost ÷ outcome. A clinic programme costing 3 million and producing 1,500 extra visits costs 3,000,000 ÷ 1,500 = 2,000 per visit. CEA compares options with the same outcome.

sections.heading: Risk and stakeholders
sections.text: Risk assessment estimates the likelihood and impact of uncertain events. Sensitivity analysis tests how the results change under different assumptions. Stakeholder analysis identifies people and groups affected by or able to influence a decision, and maps their interest and power. It helps the analyst consult early, anticipate opposition and design compensation or communication. Analysis informs judgement; it does not replace political accountability.

keyPoints: Define the policy problem as an evidence-based gap between the present and a desired situation.
State objectives that are specific, measurable, time-bound and clear about whose welfare counts.
Compare options against effectiveness, efficiency, equity and feasibility.
NPV = present value of benefits − present value of costs; BCR = present value of benefits ÷ present value of costs.
Cost per unit of outcome = cost ÷ outcome in cost-effectiveness analysis.
Risk assessment addresses uncertainty; stakeholder analysis maps interest and power.

en.title: Public Sector Economics
en.short: Covers market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, government failure and distribution.

sections.heading: Market failure
sections.text:
Public sector economics studies when government action can improve welfare and when it cannot. A market failure is a case where free exchange does not produce an efficient outcome.

Public goods are non-rival, so one person’s use does not reduce another’s, and non-excludable, so providers cannot easily charge. National defence is the standard example. Because private firms cannot capture the benefit, the good is underprovided.

sections.heading: Externalities and information
sections.text:
An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on third parties. Pollution is a negative externality; vaccination creates a positive one. A Pigouvian tax sets a charge equal to the marginal external cost, the extra harm from one more unit, aiming to make the private cost match the social cost.

Information problems arise when one side knows more. Used-car sellers know more than buyers, and patients know less than doctors. Regulation, disclosure and warranties are responses.

sections.heading: Taxation and incidence
sections.text:
Taxes raise revenue but change behaviour. A tax on a good shifts supply; part of the burden falls on buyers and part on sellers. The split depends on elasticities, meaning how strongly quantity responds to price.

Suppose a tax of 20 naira per unit raises the price buyers pay from 100 to 112 naira and lowers the price sellers keep to 92 naira. Buyers bear 12 naira and sellers bear 8 naira. Total burden is 12 + 8 = 20 naira, so the arithmetic checks. If demand is less elastic than supply, buyers bear more. The tax also reduces quantity, creating deadweight loss, the lost surplus from trades no longer made.

sections.heading: Government failure and equity
sections.text:
Government failure occurs when intervention creates inefficiency or unintended costs. Causes include weak information, lobbying, poor incentives and administrative costs.

Equity arguments concern fairness. A policy may be efficient yet leave some worse off, so analysts examine distributional effects: who gains, who pays and whether compensation is possible. Efficiency and equity often trade off, and the choice is political.

keyPoints: Market failure means free exchange does not produce an efficient outcome.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so markets tend to underprovide them.
A Pigouvian tax equals the marginal external cost and aims to align private and social costs.
Tax per unit = rise in buyer price + fall in seller price; the less elastic side bears more.
Government failure can make an intervention worse than the market problem it targets.
Efficiency and equity are separate tests; analysts should report both gains and distributional effects.

en.title: Public Budgeting and the Budget Cycle
en.short: Budget concepts, formats, the full cycle, roles, and deficits, transparency and credibility.

sections.heading: Budget concepts and formats
sections.text:
A budget is a government’s annual financial plan. It estimates revenue, authorises expenditure and sets policy priorities. The legislature passes it as an appropriation law, giving spending agencies authority to spend. Formats differ. A line-item budget lists inputs by object. A programme budget groups spending by objectives and outputs. Performance budgeting links money to results, and zero-based budgeting requires each item to be justified from zero.

A deficit occurs when planned expenditure exceeds revenue; a surplus is the reverse. Deficits are financed by borrowing, and both the deficit and the borrowing must be disclosed.

sections.heading: The budget cycle
sections.text:
The cycle has four stages. In preparation, the ministry of finance sets ceilings and calls for estimates. Agencies prepare bids, and the executive reconciles them into a draft budget. In approval, the legislature debates, amends and passes the appropriation law. In execution, agencies spend within their votes (the amounts appropriated to them), while the treasury releases cash and monitors commitments. In audit and review, the supreme audit institution examines accounts, and the legislature holds hearings.

Roles must be clear. The executive proposes and manages the budget. The legislature authorises and oversees spending. Agencies are accountable for results within their votes.

sections.heading: Deficits, transparency, credibility
sections.text: Budget credibility means the approved budget is implemented broadly as planned. It weakens when revenue forecasts are unrealistic, spending is off-budget, cash is released late or agencies overspend. Transparency means timely, clear and accessible information on revenue, expenditure, debt and performance. Without it, legislators and citizens cannot hold government to account. A deficit is not automatically bad, but it must be measured and explained. Borrowing for recurrent spending is usually riskier than borrowing for capital investment.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A ministry’s budget is ₦200 million: recurrent ₦120 million and capital ₦80 million. Expected revenue is ₦170 million, so the planned deficit is ₦30 million, or 30 ÷ 200 = 15% of expenditure. If actual revenue is ₦150 million and spending is ₦190 million, the actual deficit is ₦40 million. Revenue fell by ₦20 million and spending was ₦10 million below plan; the net deficit is ₦10 million worse. Check: 30 + 20 − 10 = 40.

keyPoints: A budget estimates revenue, authorises expenditure and sets policy priorities.
The cycle runs from preparation and approval to execution, monitoring and audit.
The executive proposes, the legislature authorises and oversees, and agencies account for results.
Budget credibility means implementing the approved budget as planned.
Planned deficit = planned expenditure − planned revenue.
Transparency requires timely public information on revenue, spending, debt and performance.

en.title: Public Financial Management and Control
en.short: Budget execution, cash management, internal controls, internal audit and fiscal reporting in government.

sections.heading: Budget execution
sections.text: Budget execution is the stage where approved estimates become actual spending. The treasury releases funds, often quarterly, against the approved budget. A commitment is a firm obligation, such as a signed purchase order, that will lead to a payment. Commitment control stops officers from promising more than the vote allows. The vote is the approved amount for a purpose. The vote book records appropriations, commitments, expenditure and payments. Cash rationing releases cash only as revenue arrives, which protects fiscal discipline when funds are short.

sections.heading: Cash and reporting
sections.text: Cash management aims to have enough cash to pay obligations on time without holding idle balances or borrowing expensively. A treasury single account (TSA) pools government bank accounts at the central bank, making balances visible and reducing idle cash. Fiscal reporting covers in-year reports and annual financial statements, which support accountability. Governments may report on a cash basis, recording only cash received and paid, or on an accrual basis, recording obligations when incurred. The International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) guide public sector reporting.

sections.heading: Controls and audit
sections.text: Internal control is the set of policies and procedures that safeguard public assets, keep records reliable and ensure compliance with rules. The COSO framework groups controls into five parts: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. Internal audit is an independent appraisal function, usually reporting to the head of the organisation or an audit committee, that tests whether controls work. It differs from external audit, which gives an opinion on the financial statements. Value for money means economy (lowest cost for the right quality), efficiency (output per input) and effectiveness (achieving intended results).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A ministry has a travel vote of ₦12,000,000. It has already issued commitments of ₦7,200,000.
Available uncommitted balance = 12,000,000 − 7,200,000 = ₦4,800,000.
A new request for ₦5,000,000 must be refused because it exceeds the balance by ₦200,000.
If the ministry later receives invoices for ₦4,500,000 of the committed items, expenditure is recorded at ₦4,500,000; the remaining commitment is ₦2,700,000.
This is a made-up example.

keyPoints: Budget execution turns approved estimates into spending through fund release and commitment control.
Available balance = appropriation − commitments.
Cash management pools cash, forecasts needs and avoids idle balances or costly borrowing.
Internal control safeguards assets and supports reliable reporting; internal audit gives independent assurance.
Fiscal reporting, on a cash or accrual basis, supports transparency and accountability.
Value for money rests on economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

en.title: Public Sector Accounting and Financial Reporting
en.short: Cash and accrual bases, public financial statements, standards, and asset and liability treatment.

sections.heading: Two bases
sections.text: Public sector accounting records and reports public money. The cash basis records transactions when cash is received or paid. The accrual basis records them when the underlying event occurs, so it recognises receivables and payables (amounts owed to and by the entity) and depreciation. Depreciation is the allocation of an asset’s cost over its useful life. Accrual gives a fuller view of financial position and cost, but needs reliable records. Cash is simpler and common where systems are weak.

sections.heading: Main statements
sections.text: Under accrual, the main statements are the statement of financial position (assets, liabilities and net assets at a date), the statement of financial performance (revenue and expenses for a period), the statement of changes in net assets, the cash flow statement and notes. Cash basis reports cash receipts and payments, often with disclosures. Many public entities use International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS), issued by the International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board. Countries may adopt, adapt or replace them with national rules, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Recognising items
sections.text: An asset is a resource controlled by the entity that has future service potential or economic benefit. A liability is a present obligation arising from a past event. Under accrual, revenue is recognised when earned, though tax revenue is difficult because the taxable event and collectability must be judged. Expenditure is recognised when incurred. Capital expenditure is capitalised and depreciated, not expensed at once.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A clinic receives a grant of 500,000 units cash. It pays salaries of 300,000 cash and owes 50,000 salaries at year end. It buys equipment for 120,000 cash and records depreciation of 20,000. Cash basis: receipts 500,000 minus payments 420,000 = surplus 80,000. Accrual: revenue 500,000 minus salaries 350,000 minus depreciation 20,000 = surplus 130,000. Assets are cash 80,000 plus equipment 100,000 = 180,000; liabilities 50,000; net assets 130,000. The two bases differ because accrual matches costs to the period.

keyPoints: Cash basis records cash received and paid; accrual records events when they occur.
Accrual statements show financial position, financial performance, changes in net assets and cash flows.
IPSAS are international public sector standards, but adoption and national rules differ by country.
Assets are controlled resources with future service potential; liabilities are present obligations from past events.
Capital expenditure is capitalised and depreciated, not expensed immediately.
In the example, accrual surplus = revenue − salaries incurred − depreciation; cash surplus = cash receipts − cash payments.

en.title: Public Procurement and Contract Management
en.short: Procurement principles, bid evaluation, contract management, disputes and integrity risks.

sections.heading: Principles and methods
sections.text: Public procurement is how public bodies buy goods, works and services. Core principles are value for money, fairness, transparency, competition and accountability. Open competitive tendering is the default for large contracts: the buyer advertises, issues tender documents and receives sealed bids. Other methods include restricted tendering (invitation to a shortlist of pre-qualified bidders), requests for quotations and direct procurement (from one supplier without competition). Which method applies depends on thresholds, meaning money limits set in law or regulation. Thresholds and rules vary by country, so check the current national law and regulator.

sections.heading: Evaluating bids
sections.text:
Bid evaluation must use criteria stated in the tender documents, not new ones. A common method scores price and quality, for example 70:30. Price score = lowest price ÷ bid price × 70. Quality is scored out of 30.

Suppose three bids: A price 100m, quality 24; B price 90m, quality 20; C price 110m, quality 28. Lowest price is 90m.
A: 90 ÷ 100 × 70 = 63; total 87.
B: 90 ÷ 90 × 70 = 70; total 90.
C: 90 ÷ 110 × 70 = 57.27; total 85.27.
B wins. These weights are illustrative, not a legal rule. Transparency requires publishing the notice, opening bids publicly, recording reasons and allowing complaints.

sections.heading: Contract management
sections.text: Contract management is the work of making sure the supplier delivers what was agreed: on time, at the agreed price and to the required standard. It covers mobilisation (the supplier getting ready to start work), monitoring, inspection, payment, variations and records. Variations are changes to scope, price or time; they need written approval and should be kept small. Poor contract management wastes money even when the tender was fair. Disputes may be settled by negotiation, mediation, arbitration or courts, depending on the contract clause.

sections.heading: Integrity and disputes
sections.text: Integrity risks include corruption, conflict of interest, bid rigging (collusion among bidders) and over-invoicing. Controls include separation of duties, declarations of interest, published awards, audit and whistleblower protection. A complaint mechanism and a standstill period (a pause before signing) help. Dispute resolution should follow the contract: negotiation first, then mediation or arbitration, then courts. Keep records, because they are evidence.

keyPoints: Public procurement should achieve value for money through fairness, competition and transparency.
Thresholds decide the procurement method and vary by country, so check the current law and regulator.
Bid evaluation must use criteria published in the tender documents.
Price score = lowest price ÷ bid price × weight; total score adds quality points.
Contract management covers delivery, payment, variations and records.
Integrity controls include separation of duties, declarations of interest and complaint mechanisms.

en.title: Human Resource Management in the Public Sector
en.short: Civil service systems, merit recruitment, pay, performance, training, labour relations and ethics in public employment.

sections.heading: Merit and recruitment
sections.text:
A civil service is the permanent, paid staff of the state, appointed on professional grounds and expected to serve different governments. Recruitment is attracting, assessing and selecting people for posts. Merit means judging applicants and staff on ability, qualifications and performance, not family, party or ethnic ties. Rules differ by country, so check the public service law.

Representation means the workforce should reflect society, including women, ethnic groups, disabled people and regions. This can conflict with strict merit if access to education and networks is unequal. Many systems use outreach, transparent criteria and training to widen the pool without lowering standards. Patronage fills posts through political or personal loyalty and weakens competence.

sections.heading: Pay and performance
sections.text:
Public pay usually combines basic salary, allowances, benefits and a pension. Many systems use graded scales with annual increments. Pay compression is a small difference between junior and senior pay; it can make promotion less attractive and push skilled staff to leave. Pay and pension rules differ by country and change, so use current official scales.

Performance management sets objectives, appraises results and links feedback to development or consequences. Public goals are multiple and sometimes conflicting, such as access, quality and cost. Fair appraisal uses published criteria, evidence and right to reply. Motivation may be intrinsic, such as public service, or extrinsic, such as pay and security.

sections.heading: Training, relations, ethics
sections.text:
Training is planned learning to build skills, from induction to leadership. Labour relations covers unions, collective bargaining over pay and conditions, and dispute resolution. Legal rules differ by country; many restrict strikes by some public servants.

Ethical conduct requires codes, conflict-of-interest rules, asset declarations and enforcement. Case: in a made-up ministry, 120 people apply for 4 clerical posts. A panel uses a test and interview, shortlists 12 and ranks them. It advertises in rural areas to widen the pool but selects on published criteria. Amina, a rural woman, is appointed on merit. Representation is pursued through outreach, not by ignoring merit.

keyPoints: Civil service systems vary by country, but merit appointment is the standard principle.
Recruitment and promotion should use published, job-related criteria and be open to review.
Pay compression can weaken incentives, while pay and pension rules change by country.
Performance management in public organisations must handle multiple and conflicting goals.
Training and labour relations need clear legal rules and fair procedures.
Ethical conduct depends on codes, conflict-of-interest rules and enforcement, not only statements.

en.title: Administrative Law and Public Administration
en.short: Legality, delegated legislation, natural justice, reasons and judicial review across legal systems.

sections.heading: Legality and delegation
sections.text:
Administrative law controls how public bodies use power. Legality means a body may do only what the law allows. A decision outside that authority is ultra vires, meaning beyond its powers. Courts ask whether the power exists, whether it was used for a proper purpose, and whether relevant matters were considered.

Delegated legislation is law made by a minister, agency or council under a parent statute, also called subsidiary legislation. It saves time but needs safeguards: publication, consultation, and legislative or judicial review. In the United Kingdom such laws are often statutory instruments; in Nigeria they are commonly called subsidiary legislation.

sections.heading: Fair procedure and reasons
sections.text:
Natural justice is the old name for procedural fairness. Its core rules are audi alteram partem, hear the other side, and nemo judex in causa sua, no one should judge a case where they are biased or interested. A person facing a decision affecting rights or interests should normally be told the case against them and allowed to answer.

A duty to give reasons is not universal. Some systems require it by statute, as South Africa’s Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000 does. In England and Wales there is no common law duty, though fairness may require reasons.

sections.heading: Judicial review and remedies
sections.text:
Judicial review is a court’s supervision of the legality of administrative action. The court reviews law and process, not the merits. Common grounds are illegality, procedural impropriety and irrationality; proportionality, whether the means fit the aim, is used in some jurisdictions and human rights cases.

Remedies vary. They include certiorari, which quashes a decision; mandamus, which orders a duty to be performed; prohibition, which stops an unlawful act; declarations, injunctions and damages.

Example: a made-up environmental agency closes Mallam Bello’s factory without a hearing. If the parent statute gives no closure power, the act is ultra vires. If it does, Bello should still be heard. A court may quash the closure and order a fresh hearing, not decide whether the factory was polluting.

keyPoints: Legality requires public bodies to act within powers granted by law; otherwise the action is ultra vires.
Delegated legislation is made under a parent statute and needs publication, consultation and review.
Natural justice requires a fair hearing and an unbiased decision maker.
A duty to give reasons depends on the jurisdiction and may be statutory or required by fairness.
Judicial review checks legality and procedure, not the merits, and remedies vary by jurisdiction.
Certiorari quashes, mandamus compels and prohibition restrains administrative action.

en.title: Ethics, Accountability and Corruption Control
en.short: Ethical frameworks, codes, conflict of interest, whistleblowing, accountability bodies and corruption control.

sections.heading: Ethical foundations
sections.text: Ethics is the study of right and wrong conduct. Public service ethics asks what officials owe to citizens, beyond obeying the law. Three frameworks help. Deontology judges an act by duty and rules, such as telling the truth. Consequentialism judges it by outcomes, such as whether a policy reduces harm. Virtue ethics asks what kind of person a good official is, stressing honesty and courage. These frameworks often point the same way, but they can conflict. Use them to justify decisions, not merely label them.

sections.heading: Codes and conflicts
sections.text: A code of conduct states expected standards: impartiality, integrity, confidentiality and proper use of public resources. A code works only with training, advice and enforcement. Conflict of interest arises when a private interest could improperly influence public duty. The usual controls are declaration, recusal (stepping aside) and separate decision-making. Whistleblowing is the disclosure of wrongdoing by an insider. Protection laws and confidential channels encourage it; retaliation discourages it.

sections.heading: Accountability institutions
sections.text: Accountability has two parts: answerability, the duty to explain decisions, and consequences for failure. Institutions include the legislature, courts, audit offices, ombudsmen and anti-corruption agencies. In Nigeria, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) are examples. Their effectiveness depends on independence, resources and political support. Formal powers on paper do not guarantee results.

sections.heading: Controlling corruption
sections.text: Corruption is commonly defined as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Control combines prevention, detection and sanctions. Prevention includes transparent rules, rotation of staff in risky posts, asset declarations and open budgets. Detection uses audits, complaints channels and investigations. Sanctions must be fair and consistent. Case: Amina, a district health officer, chairs a drug committee. Her brother bids. She declares the conflict and leaves. A colleague reports a bribe through a protected channel. The audit office investigates and refers the matter to the anti-corruption agency. Each step makes abuse harder to hide.

keyPoints: Ethics asks what officials owe citizens, not only what law permits.
A code of conduct needs training, advice and enforcement to matter.
Conflict of interest is controlled by declaration, recusal and separate decision-making.
Accountability means answerability plus consequences.
Whistleblower protection is a practical corruption-control tool.
Anti-corruption agencies need independence and resources to work.

en.title: Governance and Public Sector Institutions
en.short: How hierarchical, market and network governance work, and what good governance and capacity require.

sections.heading: Three governance modes
sections.text: Governance is the arrangements through which decisions are made, carried out and reviewed. It includes formal rules and informal practices. Public administration often mixes three modes. Hierarchy uses authority, rules and supervision: a ministry instructs a department. Market uses contracts, prices and competition: a council buys services from a firm. Network uses trust, shared goals and repeated interaction: agencies, firms, NGOs and community groups work together. Each mode has costs. Hierarchy can be slow and rigid. Markets can miss public values and create contract risk. Networks can blur responsibility. Master’s students should ask which mode fits the problem, and how the modes are combined.

sections.heading: Good governance principles
sections.text: Good governance is a contested ideal, not a single law. Common principles include transparency (decisions and information are open), participation (affected people have a voice), rule of law (rules are known, applied equally and enforced), accountability (officials answer for decisions), responsiveness and fairness. These principles support legitimacy. They also need institutions: skills, systems, budgets and reliable data. Institutional capacity is the ability to plan, staff, fund and coordinate public action over time. A principle without capacity becomes a slogan.

sections.heading: Case: water point
sections.text: Consider a made-up district council planning a water point. Officers Amina and Chidi use hierarchy to set safety standards and approve the budget. They use a market tender to hire a drilling contractor. They use a network with a water users’ committee and a local NGO to choose the site and plan maintenance. If the tender is secret, transparency fails. If the committee is ignored, participation fails. If no one checks the contractor, accountability fails. If the council lacks engineers, capacity fails. The mix can deliver, but only when rules, contracts and trust reinforce one another.

keyPoints: Governance is the arrangements for making, implementing and reviewing decisions.
Hierarchy, market and network modes each have strengths and risks, so public bodies usually mix them.
Good governance principles include transparency, participation, rule of law and accountability, but definitions vary.
Institutional capacity means having the skills, systems, budgets and data to act.
A principle without capacity is only a slogan.
In the water-point case, secrecy, exclusion or weak checking each breaks a different governance principle.

en.title: Intergovernmental Relations and Local Government
en.short: Federal and unitary systems, decentralisation, local finance, coordination and accountability.

sections.heading: Systems and powers
sections.text: Intergovernmental relations are the links between levels of government. In a federal system, the constitution divides powers between a central government and subnational units such as states or provinces, and each tier has legal authority. In a unitary system, the centre holds the main powers and may create or reform local authorities by ordinary law. Real systems vary: federal countries differ in state power, and unitary countries may decentralise deeply. The key questions are who decides, who pays and who is accountable.

sections.heading: Decentralisation
sections.text: Decentralisation transfers authority away from the centre. Deconcentration moves tasks to local offices of a central ministry, which still controls them. Delegation gives local bodies limited powers under central supervision. Devolution transfers real powers, resources and accountability to elected local governments. Devolution is the strongest form. It can improve local responsiveness, but only when councils have money, staff and clear legal duties. Otherwise local government becomes an empty shell.

sections.heading: Local government finance
sections.text: Local government finance has three main sources: own revenue such as property rates, fees and licences; transfers or grants from higher levels; and borrowing, usually for capital projects. A common problem is vertical fiscal imbalance: the centre collects most tax, while local governments carry costly duties. Grants can close the gap, but conditional grants also let higher levels steer local choices. A good grant system is predictable, transparent and matched to duties. Local accountability needs published budgets and audits.

sections.heading: Coordination and accountability
sections.text: Coordination needs clear roles, information and forums for dispute. Tools include intergovernmental agreements, conditional grants, performance reporting and audit. Accountability runs two ways: councils answer to residents, and higher levels oversee legality and standards without micromanaging. In a made-up Nigerian case, a state ministry and a local council run a health programme. The federal level sets standards and gives a conditional grant; the state adds funds and supervises; the council employs nurses and reports monthly. If the grant is delayed, services suffer, so finance and reporting rules must be agreed.

keyPoints: Federal systems divide powers constitutionally between central and subnational governments; unitary systems concentrate main powers at the centre.
Decentralisation ranges from deconcentration and delegation to devolution, with devolution giving elected local governments real powers and accountability.
Local governments need own revenue, predictable transfers and borrowing rules to match their duties.
Vertical fiscal imbalance arises when central government collects most tax while local government carries costly responsibilities.
Coordination relies on clear roles, intergovernmental agreements, conditional grants, performance reporting and audit.
Accountability runs both to local residents and upward to higher levels for legality and standards.

en.title: Public Service Delivery and Citizen Engagement
en.short: Service quality, access, equity, co-production, participation and complaints handling.

sections.heading: Quality, access and equity
sections.text:
Public service delivery is the process by which public agencies turn inputs into services people actually use: a clinic consultation, a birth certificate, a water connection. Service quality is judged on several dimensions. The SERVQUAL model of Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry names five: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles (the visible side, such as cleanliness).

Public services add two tests. Access means the service is reachable: physically, affordably, and without confusing procedures. Equity means fair treatment, both treating like cases alike and giving more help where need is greater. Responsiveness means the agency reacts to users’ needs, not only to its own routines.

sections.heading: Participation and co-production
sections.text:
Citizen participation runs from being told what will happen to actually deciding. Sherry Arnstein’s 1969 ladder of citizen participation arranges the rungs from manipulation and therapy (non-participation), through informing, consultation and placation (tokenism), to partnership, delegated power and citizen control (citizen power).

Co-production, a term associated with Elinor Ostrom, means users and agencies produce the service together: a water point committee managing a borehole, or parents helping to run a school. It can improve fit and trust, but it can also push costs onto poor users or be captured by local elites.

sections.heading: Voice and complaints
sections.text: Complaints mechanisms give users a route to report failure: registers, hotlines, published service charters stating standards, and independent bodies such as an ombudsman, for example Nigeria’s Public Complaints Commission. Albert Hirschman’s exit, voice and loyalty framework explains the difficulty: a user of a monopoly public service cannot exit, so voice must be built deliberately. Michael Lipsky’s street-level bureaucrats shows that front-line staff, working under pressure, decide in practice what service a citizen receives.

sections.heading: Case: a health centre
sections.text: In a made-up district, Ngozi manages a primary health centre. Waiting times were long, and patients complained to staff who had no power to change the rota. The district posted a service charter, opened a complaints register reviewed weekly by a committee that included two community members, and adjusted staff shifts. Waiting times fell and complaints were answered within a week. Voice needs a route, a listener and a response.

keyPoints: Service quality covers reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles.
Public services are also judged on access and equity, not only speed and courtesy.
Arnstein’s ladder separates token participation from real citizen power.
Co-production shares work between users and agencies, and can also shift costs onto users.
Monopoly services need built-in voice because users cannot exit.
Front-line staff discretion shapes the service a citizen actually receives.

en.title: Public-Private Partnerships and Infrastructure
en.short: PPP models, risk allocation, value for money, contract design and fiscal risks.

sections.heading: PPP basics
sections.text: A public-private partnership (PPP) is a long-term contract in which a private firm designs, builds, finances or operates public infrastructure or services, paid by users or government. Models include build-operate-transfer (BOT), build-own-operate (BOO), and design-build-finance-operate-maintain (DBFOM). In a concession, a private firm runs an asset, usually collecting user fees, for a set period. In an availability payment PPP, government pays only when the asset is available and meets standards. A user-pay PPP charges tolls or tariffs. Each model shifts different duties and risks.

sections.heading: Risk and value
sections.text: Risk allocation assigns each risk to the party best able to manage it. Construction cost risk may go to the private partner; demand risk may stay public if government controls tariffs. Value for money (VfM) means the best combination of cost and quality over the asset’s life. It is tested by comparing the PPP’s risk-adjusted whole-life cost with a public sector comparator (PSC), which estimates public delivery cost. Genuine risk transfer, competition and clear output specifications are essential. Contracts should link payment to performance and set out termination, dispute and change rules.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A hypothetical water plant has a PSC of 70m construction + 30m operating + 10m retained risk = 110m. A PPP bid is 65m construction + 35m operating + 8m financing = 108m. Government still retains 4m risk, so total PPP cost = 112m. The PPP is 2m worse than the PSC, so it fails the VfM test. If the bid had been 100m, total 104m, it would save 6m. Figures are illustrative.

sections.heading: Fiscal and public interest
sections.text: PPPs create fiscal risks that may not appear as immediate debt. Contingent liabilities are costs government owes only if certain events happen; they include guarantees, minimum revenue support and termination payments. Governments need affordability limits, disclosure and central approval. Regulation should protect users through quality standards and fair tariffs, and allow renegotiation without the operator capturing the process. Partnerships serve the public interest when outputs are clear, competition is real, risks are transferred only where efficient, and contract management capacity exists. They weaken where demand is uncertain, technology changes fast, or contracts are opaque.

keyPoints: A PPP is a long-term contract for infrastructure or services, paid by users or government.
Risk should go to the party best able to manage it, not simply to the private partner.
Value for money compares risk-adjusted whole-life costs, not just lowest price.
Total PPP cost = private payments + risks retained by government.
Contingent liabilities and termination payments must be disclosed and budgeted for.
Partnerships suit clear, measurable outputs with real competition and contract management capacity.

en.title: E-Government and Digital Governance
en.short: Digital public services, digital identity, data governance, inclusion, privacy and organisational change.

sections.heading: E-government and governance
sections.text: E-government is the use of information and communication technology (ICT) by public bodies to deliver services, share information and involve citizens. Digital governance is wider: the rules, institutions and practices that guide technology in public life. A useful distinction is digitisation, which turns paper into digital form, and digital transformation, which redesigns processes around users. A scanned form is digitisation; an online service that checks eligibility, takes payment and updates records is transformation. The second usually changes jobs, laws and budgets, so it is harder than buying software.

sections.heading: Identity, data and inclusion
sections.text: Digital identity is a verified representation of a person in a system, used for authentication, which proves who someone is. It can be a national identity number, a digital certificate or a biometric record. Data governance sets who may collect, use, share and delete data, and for what purpose. Interoperability means systems can exchange and use data without manual re-entry. Privacy and cybersecurity are safeguards: privacy limits collection and use, while cybersecurity protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. Inclusion requires accessible channels, offline alternatives, local languages and support for people without smartphones or reliable power. Laws on data protection differ by country, so check the current national law.

sections.heading: A concrete case
sections.text: Suppose a state health agency registers births at clinics. It issues a digital child health identifier, links records to a central register, and lets parents request certificates online. Before launch it tests with rural users, keeps paper forms, trains staff, signs data-sharing agreements and runs security audits. If it only buys software, staff still re-enter data and queues remain. The gain comes from process redesign, clear data rules and skills.

keyPoints: E-government uses ICT to deliver public services; digital governance covers the wider rules and institutions.
Digitisation converts paper to digital form, while digital transformation redesigns processes around users.
Digital identity supports authentication, and interoperability lets systems exchange data without manual re-entry.
Data governance defines who may collect, use, share and delete data, and for what purpose.
Inclusion requires accessible channels, offline alternatives and support for people with low connectivity.
Cybersecurity and privacy safeguards, plus organisational change, are essential for trustworthy digital government.

en.title: Performance Management in the Public Sector
en.short: Measuring, targeting and reviewing public performance, including incentives and unintended effects.

sections.heading: The performance cycle
sections.text:
Performance management is a repeated cycle: set objectives, choose indicators, set targets, collect data, review results and act. Performance measurement is the regular collection of data on inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes. An indicator is a variable used to judge performance, such as waiting time or the share of cases completed correctly. Outputs are what an organisation produces; outcomes are changes for citizens. A target is a desired level of performance. Benchmarking compares results with similar organisations or recognised good practice. Performance review is a structured discussion of the data, its causes and the action to take.

Public organisations usually have several goals, including equity and due process, so no single indicator can capture success. Good systems use a small balanced set of measures and check data quality.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose a clinic targets 90% of patients being seen within 30 minutes. In a month 1,000 patients attend and 810 are seen within 30 minutes. The indicator is 810 ÷ 1,000 = 81%. The target is 90%, so the gap is 9 percentage points, or 90 patients. If peer clinics average 85%, the clinic is 4 points below the benchmark. Managers should ask why: demand, staffing, triage or recording. The number alone does not prove poor management.

sections.heading: Incentives and risks
sections.text: Targets and indicators create incentives. Rewards, promotion or public ranking can focus effort, but they can also cause gaming: changing behaviour to improve the measure without improving the service. Common risks are cream-skimming easy cases, neglecting unmeasured quality, tunnel vision and misreporting. A target may also encourage short-term action at the expense of long-term outcomes. Safeguards include balanced measures, independent audit, citizen feedback, clear definitions and reviews that ask for explanation rather than blame.

sections.heading: Using the information
sections.text: Performance information should inform decisions on budgets, staffing, service design and contracts. Use it alongside context, cost data and citizen voice. A review should end with agreed actions, owners and dates. Otherwise performance management becomes reporting for its own sake.

keyPoints: Performance management links objectives, indicators, targets, review and action.
An indicator is a valid and reliable sign of performance, not the whole result.
Indicator = achieved count ÷ possible count × 100 when expressed as a percentage.
Targets and incentives can motivate effort but may cause gaming and neglect of unmeasured goals.
Benchmarking compares performance with peers or recognised good practice.
Performance reviews should explain results and agree actions, not just rank or blame.

en.title: Strategic Management in Public Organisations
en.short: Strategy formulation, stakeholder analysis, scanning, planning, implementation and performance in public agencies.

sections.heading: Strategy in public bodies
sections.text: Strategic management is the continuous work of setting direction, choosing priorities, aligning resources and reviewing results. Strategy formulation is deciding what the organisation will achieve and how, under uncertainty. Public organisations differ from firms: they pursue several goals, answer to political leaders, rely on public money and must show accountability. A useful test is public value: does the strategy improve outcomes citizens value, at a defensible cost?

sections.heading: Scanning and stakeholders
sections.text: Environmental scanning is a systematic look at outside trends and inside capacity. PESTLE covers political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors. SWOT summarises strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Stakeholder analysis identifies groups affected by or able to influence the strategy, then maps them by interest and power. In a public agency, stakeholders include citizens, ministries, staff unions and contractors. High-power, high-interest groups need close engagement; low-power groups still need a voice.

sections.heading: Planning and implementation
sections.text: Strategic planning turns direction into objectives, actions, timelines, budgets and named responsibilities. Implementation is the harder part: money, staff, skills, systems and authority must fit the plan. A simple alignment check is to map every large budget line to a strategic objective. Case: a made-up state health agency aims to raise full child immunisation from 60% to 75% in two years. Scanning flags vaccine supply risk. Stakeholder mapping shows ward heads have high interest but low power, while the health ministry has high power. The plan allocates 40% of new funds to outreach, 35% to cold chain (the refrigerated storage and transport that keep vaccines effective) and 25% to training. Check: 40 + 35 + 25 = 100%. Quarterly reviews track coverage.

sections.heading: Strategy and performance
sections.text: Strategy links to performance through a few clear indicators, targets and regular review. Outputs count, such as clinics visited, but outcomes matter more, such as immunisation coverage. Resources must follow priorities, or the plan is only words. Political priorities can shift, so managers review and adjust. Performance improves when staff see how their work supports the strategy and when leaders use evidence in decisions.

keyPoints: Strategic management sets direction, aligns resources and reviews results.
Environmental scanning uses PESTLE and SWOT to read outside trends and internal capacity.
Stakeholder analysis maps interest and power to guide engagement.
Strategic planning converts direction into objectives, actions, budgets and responsibilities.
Implementation succeeds when money, staff, skills, systems and authority align with strategy.
Strategy links to performance through a few outcome indicators and regular review.

en.title: Leadership and Change in Public Organisations
en.short: Leadership theories, change management, resistance, communication, coalitions and ethics in public services.

sections.heading: Leadership theories
sections.text: Leadership is influencing others toward shared goals. Early trait theory asked which personal qualities leaders share; it explains little alone. Behavioural studies contrasted task-focused and people-focused styles. Contingency theories, such as Fiedler’s, argue effectiveness depends on fit between style and situation. Transformational leadership (Burns, Bass) raises motivation through vision and individual consideration; transactional leadership uses rewards and sanctions; servant leadership puts followers and community first. In public organisations no single model suffices: leaders answer to ministers, legislatures, courts, staff and citizens, and must protect due process. Master’s readers should treat theories as lenses, not recipes.

sections.heading: Change and resistance
sections.text: Planned change often follows Lewin’s unfreeze, change, refreeze. Kotter’s eight steps include urgency, coalition, vision, communication, short wins and anchoring. Resistance is not simply disobedience: it can arise from fear of loss, uncertainty, habit or genuine disagreement. Leaders diagnose sources, explain reasons, invite participation, negotiate where legitimate, and use authority only when necessary. Public change must respect consultation rules and staff rights. A made-up case: Director Amina in a Nigerian state ministry proposes digital records. Staff fear job loss. She holds briefings, trains clerks as data officers, and pilots one unit. Resistance falls when the benefit and job protection are clear.

sections.heading: Communication, coalitions, ethics
sections.text: Communication is two-way: a clear message, repetition, suitable channels and listening. Coalition building means gathering stakeholders with a shared interest. Leaders map power and interest, build trust and agree common goals. Ethics is central. Public leaders hold trust and resources, so they must declare conflicts of interest, act transparently, treat people fairly and accept accountability. Ethical leadership sets the tone; codes and oversight support it. A leader who wins change by misleading staff damages public trust. The test is whether the change serves the public and respects the people who deliver it.

keyPoints: Leadership is influence toward shared public goals, not a fixed set of traits.
Contingency theories say the best leadership style depends on the situation.
Transformational leadership uses vision and individual consideration; transactional leadership uses rewards and sanctions.
Lewin’s model is unfreeze, change, refreeze; Kotter’s model adds urgency, coalition, vision and short wins.
Resistance can be legitimate; diagnose it and use communication and participation before authority.
Ethical public leadership requires transparency, fairness, conflict declaration and accountability.

en.title: Public Sector Reform
en.short: Reform ideas, design, sequencing, implementation capacity and evaluation in public organisations.

sections.heading: Reform families
sections.text: Public sector reform is deliberate change to the structures, processes, rules or culture of government. New public management (NPM) applies private-sector ideas: splitting large departments into smaller agencies, performance targets, competition and customer choice. It was popularised in the 1980s and 1990s and linked to writers such as Christopher Hood. New public governance (NPG) sees services as delivered through networks of public, private and voluntary actors. It stresses trust, negotiation and co-production, where citizens help design and deliver services. Whole-of-government or joined-up approaches try to coordinate agencies around shared outcomes instead of separate targets.

sections.heading: Design and sequencing
sections.text: Reform design starts with a clear problem and a theory of change: the chain from inputs to activities, outputs and outcomes. Designers map stakeholders, legal authority, costs and risks. Sequencing matters. A common order is to secure political support, build basic systems, pilot in one area, then scale. Jumping to large-scale restructuring before capacity exists often fails. Context includes history, informal rules, fiscal space (room in the budget) and administrative capacity, meaning the skills, data and systems needed to carry the reform.

sections.heading: Implementation and capacity
sections.text: Implementation is where reform usually stalls. It needs capable leaders, stable funding, reliable data and staff who understand the change. Principal-agent problems arise when central reformers cannot observe local behaviour. Street-level bureaucrats, the frontline staff who deal directly with citizens, may adapt or resist rules. A realistic plan allows training, communication and time. Capacity building is not only training; it includes pay, equipment, information systems and authority to decide.

sections.heading: Evaluation and case
sections.text: Evaluation asks whether the reform caused change, not only whether change occurred. Useful methods include before-and-after measures, comparison groups and process tracing, which follows the steps linking reform to result. A hypothetical case: a Nigerian state creates a citizen service centre to combine permit services from three ministries. It first maps legal powers, trains staff, and pilots one centre for six months. After the pilot it compares processing times and complaints, then scales only if queues and error rates fall. This shows design, sequencing, capacity and evaluation together.

keyPoints: NPM uses private-sector tools such as performance targets, competition and customer choice.
NPG emphasises networks, trust and co-production among public, private and voluntary actors.
Whole-of-government approaches coordinate agencies around shared outcomes.
Reform design needs a clear problem, theory of change and stakeholder analysis.
Sequencing and administrative capacity often decide whether reform succeeds.
Evaluation should test causal change, not just report activity.

en.title: Programme Evaluation
en.short: Evaluation questions, process and impact designs, indicators, and using findings for learning and accountability.

sections.heading: Framing the evaluation
sections.text: Programme evaluation is the systematic, evidence-based judgement of a public programme’s design, implementation and results. It starts with evaluation questions: what decision will the evidence inform, and for whom? Useful questions cover relevance, implementation, outcomes and value for money. A theory of change or logic model sets out how inputs become activities, outputs, outcomes and impact. It makes assumptions visible and shows where evidence is needed.

sections.heading: Process and impact
sections.text: Process evaluation examines whether activities were delivered as planned: reach, fidelity, quality and barriers. Impact evaluation asks whether outcomes changed because of the programme, not merely after it. The counterfactual is what would have happened without it. Attribution is the share of change plausibly caused by the programme; contribution accepts that other factors also matter. Example: a fictional district health scheme gives pregnant women free transport. Process evaluation checks how many women used it and why others did not. Impact evaluation compares facility birth rates between women covered by the scheme and a similar group outside it.

sections.heading: Designs and indicators
sections.text: Indicators are measurable signs of an activity, output or outcome; they need clear definitions, baselines and targets. Designs include randomised controlled trials (RCTs), where eligible units are assigned by chance to treatment or comparison groups; quasi-experimental designs, such as difference-in-differences or matching, when randomisation is impossible; and simple before-after studies, which are weak for attribution. A mixed-methods design combines administrative data, surveys and interviews. Ethical approval and consent are essential.

sections.heading: Using findings
sections.text: Findings should be reported against the questions, with limitations and uncertainty stated. They support accountability to citizens and funders, policy learning and programme improvement. Learning requires timely feedback, discussion with implementers and users, and a clear response: continue, adjust, scale or stop. Evaluation is political, so independence and transparency protect credibility.

keyPoints: Evaluation questions should be tied to decisions and users before data are collected.
Process evaluation checks delivery, reach and fidelity; impact evaluation tests whether outcomes changed because of the programme.
The counterfactual is the comparison of what would have happened without the programme.
Randomised controlled trials give strong attribution; quasi-experimental designs are used when randomisation is not possible.
Indicators need clear definitions, baselines and targets.
Findings should feed accountability, policy learning and programme improvement, with limitations stated.

en.title: Quantitative Methods for Public Administration
en.short: Descriptive statistics, probability, sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and regression for policy.

sections.heading: Summarising data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics reduce a dataset to useful numbers. The mean is the arithmetic average; the median is the middle value when data are ordered; the mode is the most frequent value. Range, variance and standard deviation measure spread. Use the median for skewed data, where values stretch into a long tail on one side. Probability gives an event a number from 0 to 1 and supports risk statements. A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, such as a mean, over repeated samples.

sections.heading: Sampling and testing
sections.text: Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; simple random sampling is the basic form. Sampling error is variation from using a sample rather than the whole population. Bias is systematic error, such as excluding rural households. A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter. A 95% CI means that if sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. It is not a 95% probability that the parameter lies in this interval. Hypothesis testing compares a null hypothesis (a default claim, such as no difference) with data. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as observed if the null is true. Compare it with a chosen significance level, often 0.05, and reject the null when the p-value is smaller. A small p-value is evidence against the null, not proof.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose 100 households have mean monthly water spending ₦4,000 and sample standard deviation ₦1,000. Standard error = 1,000 ÷ √100 = 100. The 95% CI is 4,000 ± 1.96 × 100 = 4,000 ± 196, or ₦3,804 to ₦4,196. Test H0: mean = ₦3,800 against a two-sided alternative. z = (4,000 − 3,800) ÷ 100 = 2.00. Since 2.00 exceeds 1.96, reject H0 at 5%; the p-value is about 0.046. Regression links a dependent variable to independent variables. In y = 10 + 0.5x, a one-unit rise in x is associated with a 0.5-unit rise in y. R² is the share of variation in y explained. Association is not causation.

keyPoints: Descriptive statistics summarise centre and spread; use the median for skewed data.
Standard error = sample standard deviation ÷ √n.
95% CI = estimate ± 1.96 × standard error for large samples.
z = (estimate − hypothesised value) ÷ standard error; compare with critical values or a p-value.
Regression coefficient gives the change in y for a one-unit change in x, other things equal.
R² is the share of variation in y explained; association is not causation.

en.title: Research Methods in Public Administration
en.short: Research design, sampling, data collection, analysis, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Design and literature
sections.text: A research design is the plan that links a question to evidence. It states the purpose, concepts, method and limits. A literature review is not a list of summaries. It shows what is known, where studies disagree and which gap your question addresses. Use credible sources and record every citation. Quantitative designs test measurable relationships with numbers and statistics. Qualitative designs explore meaning, experience and process through words and observation. Mixed methods combine both when the question needs it. A good design is feasible, ethical and able to answer the question.

sections.heading: Sampling and data
sections.text: Sampling is choosing cases from a population, the whole group your question is about. Probability sampling gives every case a known chance of selection, so results can be generalised. Common types are simple random sampling, systematic sampling (every kth case after a random start) and stratified sampling, which divides the population into groups, such as units, and samples from each. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or convenience sampling, is used in qualitative work but limits generalisation. Data collection may use surveys, interviews, focus groups, documents or observation. A case: a ministry has 1,200 staff in units of 600, 400 and 200. For a sample of 120, the fraction is 120 ÷ 1,200 = 10%. Proportional allocation gives 60, 40 and 20. Check: 60 + 40 + 20 = 120.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text: Analysis matches the design. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics and, where justified, inferential tests. Qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis: coding text, grouping codes into themes and checking them against the data. Keep an audit trail. Research ethics protect people and knowledge. Seek informed consent, avoid harm, protect privacy and confidentiality, and let participants withdraw. Get ethical approval. Do not fabricate, falsify or plagiarise. Cite others and report methods honestly.

sections.heading: Writing the report
sections.text: A report or dissertation has a title, abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, findings, discussion, conclusion and references. The methods chapter explains sampling, instruments and analysis so another researcher could repeat the work. The discussion links findings to the literature and states limitations. Write plainly, define terms, and use tables when they help. Check the university’s style guide and submission rules.

keyPoints: A research design links the question, evidence, method and limits.
A literature review identifies what is known, disagreements and the gap you address.
Probability sampling gives every case a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling does not.
Sampling fraction = sample size ÷ population size; proportional allocation uses each stratum’s share.
Quantitative analysis uses statistics, while qualitative analysis often uses coding and themes.
Ethics require informed consent, no harm, confidentiality, honest reporting and no plagiarism.

en.title: Comparative Public Administration
en.short: Compares public administration systems, reform experiences, state capacity, policy transfer and the limits of comparison.

sections.heading: What comparison studies
sections.text: Comparative public administration studies how public administration systems differ and why. A system includes the institutions that make and carry out public decisions: ministries, agencies, local government and the civil service. Comparison may focus on structures, processes, values, reform experiences or results. It is not a list of countries. The aim is to explain similarities and differences using context: history, culture, law, economy and political settlement. A useful comparison states the unit, such as country, sector or organisation, the time period and the criteria. Without these, claims that one country is more efficient cannot be tested.

sections.heading: Context and capacity
sections.text: Culture and history shape how administration works. Colonial legacies, legal traditions and patterns of state formation influence institutions. State capacity means the ability of the state to collect revenue, enforce rules and deliver services across its territory. It varies within countries as well as between them. A reform that works where capacity is high may fail where staff, data and funding are scarce. Comparative analysis therefore asks whether a practice depends on conditions that cannot be copied easily. It also distinguishes formal rules from actual behaviour, because laws on paper may be weakly enforced.

sections.heading: Transfer and limits
sections.text: Policy transfer is the movement of ideas, policies or institutions from one setting to another.
