Lesson drawing is voluntary learning; coercion is imposition by donors, creditors or colonial powers. Transfer often fails when context is ignored. A concrete case: a made-up country, Kanda, imports a digital procurement system from a high-capacity country. The software works, but suppliers lack internet access and auditors lack training, so use is low. The lesson is to compare functions, not just forms, and to pilot before scaling. Comparison also has limits: concepts may not translate, data may be unreliable, and the observer’s own assumptions may distort the picture. Good comparative work is explicit about these limits.

keyPoints: Comparative public administration explains differences between systems using context, not simple rankings.
State capacity is the state’s ability to collect revenue, enforce rules and deliver services.
Policy transfer is the movement of ideas or institutions across settings.
Lesson drawing is voluntary learning; coercion is imposed transfer.
Comparison must state its unit, period and criteria, and distinguish formal rules from actual behaviour.
Transfer should compare functions and context, and pilot before scaling.

en.title: Development Administration: State Capacity, Policy and Aid
en.short: State capacity, development policy, aid relationships and coordination in development administration.

sections.heading: Meaning and scope
sections.text: Development administration is the part of public administration concerned with using state organisations to raise living standards, not just to keep order. It studies how ministries, agencies and local governments plan, coordinate and deliver development policy. A key idea is state capacity: the ability of the state to decide, collect revenue, implement decisions and learn. Capacity has administrative, fiscal, technical and political sides. Weak capacity shows up as poor coordination, delayed projects and rules that cannot be enforced.

sections.heading: Policy and the state
sections.text: Development policy covers choices about growth, jobs, health, education and infrastructure. Public administrators advise on these choices and turn them into programmes. Some writers point to a developmental state, where the state guides investment and industrial policy. Others stress that policy must be owned locally and fit local institutions. A state that copies foreign models without adapting them may build formal plans that are not implemented.

sections.heading: Aid and coordination
sections.text: Aid relationships link developing-country governments with donors and lenders. Aid can fund services and advice, but it can also fragment budgets and weaken local accountability. The Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness (2005) set principles such as country ownership, alignment with national plans and harmonisation among donors. These are voluntary principles, not binding law. Coordination is hard because many actors have different timetables and reporting rules.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider a made-up case in a district in Ghana. A donor funds boreholes, the district assembly owns the water plan, and the health ministry runs hygiene campaigns. Without one coordinating committee, boreholes are drilled where access is easy, not where need is greatest. A simple fix is a joint district plan with one budget line and one reporting format. Institutional reform also matters: clear roles for the assembly, the water agency and community committees, plus maintenance funds after the donor leaves.

keyPoints: Development administration uses public organisations to pursue development goals, not only routine administration.
State capacity includes the fiscal, administrative, technical and political ability to decide and implement policy.
Development policy must be locally owned and adapted to local institutions.
Aid can fund services but may fragment budgets and weaken accountability.
The Paris Declaration principles are voluntary, so donors and governments may not follow them.
Clear roles, joint plans and maintenance funds help coordination and institutional reform.

en.title: Nonprofit and Civil Society Management
en.short: Governance, funding, accountability and state relations in nonprofits, NGOs and civil society.

sections.heading: Sector and forms
sections.text:
A nonprofit is an organisation that pursues a mission and does not distribute surplus to owners. Civil society is broader: community groups, faith bodies, unions, professional associations and NGOs.

An NGO is a nongovernmental organisation, often delivering services or advocacy. Forms and registration differ by country, so check the national law. Common legal forms include charity, trust, association and company limited by guarantee. A social enterprise is not a legal form but a trading model that can take any of these, and it reinvests most profit into the mission.

sections.heading: Governance and accountability
sections.text:
Governance is the system of direction and control. A board of trustees or directors guards the mission, approves strategy and budgets, oversees risk and appoints the chief executive.

Accountability runs in several directions: upward to regulators and donors, downward to beneficiaries and communities, and inward to members and staff. Practical tools include audited accounts, annual reports, conflict-of-interest rules, safeguarding policies and complaints channels. Legitimacy also depends on participation, transparency and evidence that promises were kept.

sections.heading: Funding and donors
sections.text:
Funding comes from grants, government contracts, donations, membership fees, trading and social investment. Each source carries conditions. Restricted grants may be spent only on named activities.

Government contracts can support public services but may pull an organisation toward administrative work and away from advocacy. Donors often require reports, evaluations and procurement rules. A sound funding plan diversifies income to reduce dependency, keeps reserves, and states clearly how overhead costs are covered. Advocacy needs independent resources, because donors may limit political activity.

sections.heading: Case: community NGO
sections.text:
Case: Sahel Health Trust, a fictional community NGO in Kano, Nigeria, runs maternal health outreach. It has seven trustees, a government service contract, a donor training grant and community contributions. The contract pays core staff, the grant is restricted to training, and community cash is unrestricted.

When a donor payment is late, the trust uses its reserve and the board reviews the risk. It publishes audited accounts and holds an annual community meeting. The case shows how governance, funding rules and accountability to different parties interact.

keyPoints: Nonprofits pursue a mission and do not distribute surplus to owners.
Civil society includes NGOs, community groups, faith bodies, unions and professional associations.
A board guards the mission and oversees strategy, finance and risk.
Accountability runs upward to donors and regulators, downward to communities and inward to members and staff.
Restricted grants and government contracts carry conditions that can shape or distort a mission.
Legal forms and registration rules vary by country, so check the national law.

en.title: Public Administration Capstone Project
en.short: Designing, doing and presenting an applied public administration project or dissertation.

sections.heading: From topic to problem
sections.text:
A capstone answers a question about real administrative practice, not a general topic. Turn a broad concern into a researchable problem: what exactly is going wrong, for whom, and what would count as an answer? Write a problem statement, two or three research questions, and the scope you will not cover.

Case: Amina, an MPA student in Kano, wanted to study poor service delivery. She narrowed it to waiting times for business permits at one state licensing office, and to the views of staff and applicants. That is feasible in one semester.

sections.heading: Literature and design
sections.text:
The literature review is an argument, not a list of summaries. Group sources by theme, show where they agree and disagree, and end with the gap your project addresses. A conceptual framework sets out the factors you expect to matter.

Choose a design that fits the question: a case study for how and why, a survey for how widespread, secondary data for trends. Explain sampling, your instruments, and how you will guard validity (measuring what you claim) and reliability (repeatability). Obtain ethics approval and informed consent, and follow data protection law, such as the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

sections.heading: Analysis and recommendations
sections.text:
Analysis follows the questions. Qualitative data is usually coded into themes; quantitative data is described with counts and averages, and tested where justified. Report what you found, including surprises.

Recommendations are not findings. Each should name the actor responsible, the action, the resource needed, and the evidence behind it. 'Improve service delivery' is not a recommendation; 'publish permit waiting times monthly at the front desk' is.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text:
Follow the required structure: introduction, literature, methods, findings, discussion, recommendations, references. Cite every borrowed idea; plagiarism checks are strict. Length and format rules differ by institution, so check your handbook.

Rehearse the defence: state your question, method, main finding and recommendation in five minutes, and expect questions on sampling and bias. Keep a dated log of supervisor meetings.

keyPoints: A capstone turns a broad concern into a researchable question with a stated scope.
The literature review builds an argument that ends in the gap your project fills.
The design must fit the question: case study, survey or secondary data.
Ethics approval, informed consent and data protection law apply to student projects.
Each recommendation names an actor, an action, a resource and the evidence behind it.
The defence is a short, clear account of question, method, finding and recommendation.
